## 2 Results and Discussion

The hierarchical porous carbons (SC-HPCs and SCR-HPCs) were synthesized using SC and its decoction residue (SCR) as precursors via a combined pre-carbonization and KOH activation strategy (Figure 1a). SC, as a typical medicinal herb, possesses a lignocellulosic matrix (cellulose/hemicellulose/lignin complex) with a high content of organic active ingredients (tannins, polyphenols, saponins, etc.^{[}^{22}^{]}) that results in a distinctive biomass texture. Decoction pretreatment has been demonstrated to induce cell wall rupture and the release of active ingredients through a concentration gradient mass transfer effect, as well as to promote the decomposition of the lignin–carbohydrate complex (LCC).^{[}^{23-25}^{]} This process establishes critical structural templates that facilitate the oriented growth of graphitic crystallites and the construction of a hierarchical porous structure during subsequent activation.

Figure 1

Open in figure viewerPowerPoint

a) Schematic of the preparation of SC-HPCs and SCR-HPCs, b–e) SEM images, f, g) EDS mappings of C, O, and N, h) N_{2} adsorption–desorption isotherms, i) pore size distribution, j, k) high-resolution XPS spectra of C 1s, and l, m) high-resolution XPS spectra of O 1s of SC and SCR samples.

Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) images (Figure 1b–e) clearly reveal that both SC and SCR exhibit the raw SC unique 3D honeycomb-like porous structure, indicating their natural porosity. However, following decoction pretreatment, a significant change in the microstructure of the SCR was observed, with surface tissues separating to form a more loose skeletal structure (see Figure S1a,b, Supporting Information for cross-sections). Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS) verifies that the SC and SCR surfaces are mainly composed of carbon (C), oxygen (O), and nitrogen (N) (Figure 1f,g). The pore structure of SC and SCR was further investigated using N_{2} adsorption/desorption at 77 K. As shown in Figure 1h,i, the decoction pretreatment raises the SSA from 12.3 m^{2} g^{−1} (SC) to 28.8 m^{2} g^{−1} (SCR), and increases mesopore numbers in the 2.4–8 nm range, demonstrating effective SSA and porosity optimization in SCR. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) analysis (Figure S2a–c, Supporting Information) reveals the distinct chemical structures of lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose in both the SC and SCR samples.^{[}^{26}^{]} Decoction pretreatment resulted in partial bond scission and reorganization of the cellulose and hemicellulose in the samples.^{[}^{27}^{]} Also, the lignin aromatic ring conjugation system was partially disrupted and the hydroxyl hydrogen-bonding network was weakened.^{[}^{14}^{]} The effect of decoction pretreatment on the chemical composition and bonding configuration of the SC surface was further evaluated by using X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) spectroscopy (Figure S3, Supporting Information). This indicates a significant antagonistic effect between porosity and graphitization in the structural development of porous carbon materials. In this study, the I_{D}/I_{G} ratios of SC-HPCs (1.11 at 800 °C, 1.17 at 900 °C, and 1.07 at 1000 °C) remain highly consistent with this statistical pattern. In contrast, the SCR-HPCs, which underwent decoction pretreatment, exhibit significant variations: the ratio rises to 1.38 at 800 °C (indicating more pronounced disordered etching), declines sharply to 0.73 at 900 °C (reflecting synergy between pore development and graphite microcrystal assembly), and falls further to 0.36 at 1000 °C (corresponding to the formation of long-range ordered graphitic domains), thereby systematically deviating from the statistical trend. Such a temperature gradient response feature reveals that pretreatment, through structural engineering of precursors, effectively decouples the kinetic competition between porosity formation and graphitization in conventional processes.

Based on the above experimental results, the formation mechanism of porous graphitic carbon can be rationally inferred. The KOH activation of carbon materials involves multiple mechanisms: 1) chemical etching by KOH and its derivatives (e.g., K_{2}CO_{3} and K_{2}O) generates hierarchical porosity, 2) physical activation via gaseous products (CO_{2} and H_{2}O) optimizes pore structure, and 3) catalytic graphitization through the intercalation of potassium into carbon lattices.^{[}^{21, 35}^{]} During activation, KOH preferentially reacts with sp^{3}-C and oxygen-containing groups in the carbon matrix and undergoes a disordered etching from the outside to the inside, which mainly produces K_{2}CO_{3}.^{[}^{19, 35}^{]} As etching proceeds, the sp^{3}-C and oxygen-containing functional groups in the carbon matrix are gradually consumed, resulting in an increase in the number of graphite microcrystals unconstrained by sp^{3}-C. This, in turn, provides a greater quantity of feedstock for the graphitization process. Additionally, the disorder of the structure is further exacerbated by gases (e.g., CO_{2} and H_{2}O) produced by violent reactions on the outer surface. Conversely, the etching effect of KOH within the internal macropores may be less pronounced, and graphite microcrystals have the opportunity to undergo ordered reorganization to form graphene nanoribbons. In the case of SCR-HPCs, the microstructure and chemical composition of the raw SC were changed by pretreatment, constructing a hierarchical porous structure enriched with reactive functional groups (sp^{3}–C, C=O, etc.) in the carbon matrix. Such a structure could provide abundant active sites and exposure interfaces for subsequent KOH activation. More importantly, the interconnected porous structure facilitates the uniform diffusion and reaction mass transport and eliminates the concentration gradient of the activator, achieving synergistic optimization of the porous structure development and graphitization, thereby creating favorable conditions for the storage and transfer of charges, which is expected to achieve a superior electrochemical energy storage.

## 3 Conclusion

This study demonstrates a simple and efficient “win-win” strategy for converting Sargentodoxa Cuneata residue (SCR) into hierarchical porous graphitic carbon. Structural characterizations indicate that the decoction pretreatment can effectively modulate the microstructure and chemical composition of raw SC and construct a hierarchical porous architecture rich in active functional groups in biochar, providing abundant active sites and exposed interfaces for the subsequent activation process, which is conducive to the promotion of graphitization of carbon materials while maintaining a high porosity. The optimized SCR-HPC-900 exhibits a high SSA (2465.1 m^{2} g^{−1}), a hierarchical porous structure (V_{Tol} of 1.27 cm^{3} g^{−1}), as well as a significant degree of graphitization (I_{D}/I_{G} of 0.73 and I_{2D}/I_{G} of 0.50). The SCR-HPC-900 electrode exhibits a high specific capacitance of 415.6 F g^{−1} at 0.5 A g^{−1} in a three-electrode system with 6 m KOH. Impressively, it remains at 312.0 F g^{−1} (75.1%) even at an ultra-high current density of 200 A g^{−1}. The fabricated symmetric supercapacitor achieves an energy density of 8.5 Wh kg^{−1} at a high power density of 37 803 W kg^{−1} and a capacitance retention of 100.8% after 100 000 cycles, demonstrating excellent rate performance and cycling stability. Additionally, the assembled supercapacitors in organic electrolytes obtain the maximum energy density and power density of 45.6 Wh kg^{−1} and 41 750 W kg^{−1}, respectively. This study develops a strategy based on precursor structural engineering, revealing the intrinsic synergistic mechanism between the porous structure development and graphitization enhancement in carbon materials, offering new insights for the development of high-performance carbon materials.

## 4 Experimental Section

#### Materials

Sargentodoxa Cuneata (SC) for the experiment was collected from Qiandongnan Prefecture, Guizhou Province, China. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) and hydrochloric acid (HCI) were purchased from Aladdin Life Science Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China. All chemicals were used without further purification.

#### Synthesis of SCR-HPCs/SC-HPCs

Fresh SC was cut into pieces (~10 cm), washed thoroughly with deionized (DI) water, and then dried at 105 °C for 24 h.

SCR-HPCs were synthesized via a combined carbonization and chemical activation strategy. Specifically, 50 g of dried SC was immersed in a ceramic pot reactor with DI water and decocted at 100 °C for 1 h under atmospheric pressure, with periodic water replenishment to ensure complete submersion. Subsequently, the residue was washed and filtered with DI water, then dried at 105 °C for 24 h to obtain SCR. Next, the dried SCR was placed in a horizontal tube furnace and heated to 700 °C at 5 °C min^{−1} under a nitrogen atmosphere for pyrolytic carbonization for 3 h. After carbonization, the material was naturally cooled, repeatedly washed with 1 m HCl and DI water, and finally dried at 80 °C for 12 h to yield Sargentodoxa Cuneata residue-derived biochar (SCR-BC).

The pre-carbonized SCR-BC was mixed with KOH at a mass ratio of 1:2 and then heated to 800, 900, and 1000 °C, respectively, at a ramp rate of 5 °C min^{−1} in the same tube furnace device and held for 3 h for activation. Finally, the resulting porous carbon samples were thoroughly washed and filtered with 20 wt.% hydrochloric acid (HCl) solution and DI water to remove impurities, then dried at 80 °C for 24 h. The dried samples were subjected to physicochemical characterization and labeled SCR-HPC-X (where X denotes the activation temperature).

As controls, parallel experiments using raw Sargentodoxa Cuneata (SC) without decoction pretreatment were conducted under identical conditions, with products designated as SC-HPC-X. This comparative design enables systematic evaluation of the structural modifications induced by decoction on porous carbon properties.

Material characterization and electrochemical measurement are provided in the Supporting Information.

## Abstract and Figures

Activated carbon derived from spent coffee grounds is synthesized by chemical activation with a defined KOH concentration and varying urea concentration. The effects of urea concentration on porosity development, electrical conductivity, and charge storage performance are systematically evaluated using SEM, Raman, XRD, BET, TEM, and electrochemical characterization methods. The sample activated with a 1:2:1 of carbon:KOH:urea ratio (ACKU1) exhibits the highest specific surface area (SBET = 2805 m² g⁻¹) and the most favorable pore structure, combining micro‐ and mesoporosity, whereas the sample without urea, 1:2 of carbon:KOH ratio, shows a much smaller specific surface area (SBET = 1357 m² g⁻¹). --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

摘要

* * *

The antagonism between porosity and graphitization critically limits carbon supercapacitor performance. Here, we demonstrate a structural engineering strategy that converts Sargentodoxa Cuneata residue (SCR) into hierarchically porous graphitic carbons (SCR‐HPCs). By precisely regulating biomass precursor porous architecture, this methodology decouples the antagonism between porosity development and graphitization progression in KOH‐mediated activation, achieving simultaneous high specific surface area (2465.1 m 2 g −1 ) and graphitization (I D /I G of 0.73). In 6 m KOH electrolyte, the specific capacitance of the optimized SCR‐HPC‐900 electrode reaches 415.6 F g −1 at 0.5 A g −1 , with a capacitance retention of 75.1% even at an ultra‐high current density of 200 A g −1 . The fabricated symmetric supercapacitor achieves an energy density of 8.5 Wh kg −1 at a power density of 37 803 W kg −1 , retaining over 100.8% of its capacitance after 100 000 cycles. Remarkably, in 1 m TEABF 4 /PC organic electrolyte, the supercapacitor achieves maximum energy and power densities of 45.6 Wh kg −1 and 41 750 W kg −1 , respectively. This study presents an effective methodology for decoupling the antagonism between porosity and graphitization in conventional processes, offering a new idea for converting biomass waste into high‐performance energy storage materials.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
